name: Mark Zuckerberg
title: The Kid Who Kept Saying No
subtitle: From a Risk game coded in sixth grade to a Harvard dorm room and total control of Meta: how Mark Zuckerberg builds, refuses to sell, and sometimes gets it badly wrong.
hook: As a high-school senior at Phillips Exeter Academy, Mark Zuckerberg and his friend Adam D'Angelo built a free music player called Synapse that learned what you liked to hear. After the tech site Slashdot wrote about it in April 2003, one company offered them ==$950,000==, on one condition: work for it for three years. His answer: "We wanted to go to college, so we said no." When the pair later changed their minds, the buyer had lost interest. Less than a year after that refusal, on ==4 February 2004==, he launched thefacebook.com from his Harvard dorm.

glance.label: Born
glance.value: 14 May 1984, USA (he turned 28 the same week Facebook went public)

glance.label: Grew up
glance.value: Dobbs Ferry, a town in Westchester County, New York; local Ardsley High School until his junior year, then Phillips Exeter Academy because Ardsley lacked advanced computer and maths courses

glance.label: First code
glance.value: Got his first computer in sixth grade; his first big program was a Risk-style strategy game set in the ancient Roman Empire

glance.label: First product
glance.value: Synapse, a free music player that learned your taste, built with Adam D'Angelo at Exeter; he turned down a $950,000 offer that came with a three-year job

glance.label: Education
glance.value: Studied computer science at Harvard and left without graduating to run Facebook; Harvard gave him an honorary Doctor of Laws in 2017

glance.label: First company (age)
glance.value: thefacebook.com, launched on Wednesday 4 February 2004 from his Kirkland House dorm, aged 19; over 650 Harvard students signed up within days

glance.label: Main role today
glance.value: Founder, Chairman and CEO of Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp). Controls 60.8% of shareholder votes through special 10-vote shares, and takes a salary of $1 a year

glance.label: Net worth
glance.value: $210.5 billion, #6 in the world (Forbes real-time estimate, 29 October 2026); owns about 13% of Meta; self-made

glance.label: Family (public basics)
glance.value: Met Priscilla Chan at a Harvard party in a bathroom queue; married her on 19 May 2012, the day after Facebook's IPO, at a backyard party guests thought was her graduation celebration. Three children

glance.label: Lives in / gives
glance.value: Palo Alto, California. Co-founded the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative with Chan in 2015, pledging 99% of their Meta shares over their lifetimes

contact.howToReach: There is no public personal email for Mark Zuckerberg, and nothing you send to Meta's switchboard or inboxes will be passed to him just because you asked. The doors that really open are narrow: journalists can write to press@meta.com, shareholders to investor@meta.com, and anyone with a serious governance concern can post a letter to Meta's Corporate Secretary, which Meta says can be sent anonymously or confidentially. If your Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp account has a problem, use the Meta Help Centre; the press and investor inboxes are for reporters and shareholders, not for account problems. His public posts on Facebook, Instagram and Threads are the only place he speaks directly, so a sharp comment there is your only open line, but expect no reply, and treat any account that messages you in his name offering money or jobs as fake. If you write to any of these teams, keep it under 120 words: who you are, the one specific thing you want, and why that team is the right one.

factCheck.method: Contact details were taken only from Meta's own SEC filings (2025 annual report and Form 10-K, 2026 proxy statement), Meta's investor-relations, newsroom and leadership pages, and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and Biohub websites, checked on 29 October 2026. Personal social accounts are those linked from Meta's official leadership page, plus the X account @finkd, checked on the profile itself. Biographical facts come from The Harvard Crimson's 2003-2004 reporting (read in full, quotes checked word for word), Zuckerberg's 2017 Harvard Commencement speech as published by the Harvard Gazette, CBS News, and Forbes. Photos and licences were checked through the Wikimedia Commons API. Note: the web-search budget ran out mid-research, so some lead sources (New Yorker, Vox, The Independent, Britannica) could not be opened and their claims were dropped.

disputed.claim: How much the Synapse music player was offered for, and whether it was sold
disputed.note: The Harvard Crimson (October 2003) quotes Zuckerberg saying one company offered $950,000 plus a three-year job and they said no. A June 2004 Crimson profile quotes him saying offers went 'up to one million' and then 'like two million', names AOL, WinAmp and Microsoft as interested, and says that when the pair later tried to accept, the company had lost interest. A 2011 Atlantic Wire piece says he sold Synapse to Microsoft for $950,000; both Crimson articles, written at the time, contradict that, so we use the $950,000 offer that was refused.

disputed.claim: Birthplace (often given as White Plains, New York)
disputed.note: Widely repeated, but the sources that support it (The Independent, New York magazine) could not be opened in this research pass, so the glance gives only the birth date and his hometown of Dobbs Ferry, which The Harvard Crimson confirms.
